sentences.text: Dimorphodon exhibited primitive characteristics, including a very small braincase and proportionally short wings that offered very little gliding potential.
Adult Dimorphodon measured about 1 meter in body length with a wingspan of 1.45 meters, though other estimates place the total length at 1 meter including the tail and the wingspan at 1.4 meters.
The animal possessed a long tail composed of thirty vertebrae and a large, bulky skull about 23 cm long that was lightened by large openings separated by thin bony partitions.
Research suggests that Dimorphodon's poor flying ability was a developed trait rather than an ancestral characteristic.

Dimorphodon had an elongated, clawless fifth toe oriented to the side, and it was a competent climber with proportionally large and curved claws that probably moved in a saltatorial, or leaping, manner while climbing.
It had a strong and flexible beak that may have possessed a lower membranous pouch.
The holotype specimen of Dimorphodon, NHMUK PV R1034, is a partial and disarticulated skeleton that lacks a skull.
The species name macronyx refers to the large claws on the hand of the animal.
The species name D. weintraubi honors Dr. Robert L. Weintraub, and the well-preserved foot of this specimen shows that pterosaurs had a plantigrade gait rather than a digitigrade posture.
The first fossils attributed to Dimorphodon were discovered by Mary Anning at Lyme Regis, Dorset, in December 1828.
The genus Dimorphodon was named by Richard Owen in 1859, and the genus authority is Owen, 1859.
Richard Owen found two new specimens of Dimorphodon in 1858 that included skulls, which were previously missing from earlier finds.
Dimorphodon macronyx, described by Buckland in 1829, is the type species of the genus.

Recent studies suggest Dimorphodon likely hunted small vertebrates while also consuming small invertebrates like insects, and dental microwear examinations confirm it was a vertebrate predator, though it may have occasionally eaten softer invertebrates.
Dimorphodon's teeth suggest it had a piscivorous diet, similar to many other pterosaurs.
Dimorphodon may also have hunted small terrestrial animals.
Dimorphodon was a competent climber with proportionally large and curved claws.
Like modern squirrels, Dimorphodon probably moved in a saltatorial, or leaping, manner while climbing.
In 1870, Seeley assigned Dimorphodon to its own family, Dimorphodontidae.

Dimorphodon lived in Europe during the Early Jurassic Period, approximately 201 to 191 million years ago, though other estimates place the time range from 195 to 190 million years ago or from the Hettangian to the Pliensbachian (201.4 to 184.2 million years ago).
Fossil remains of Dimorphodon have been found in England, and the animal probably lived in coastal regions.

Researchers have debated whether Dimorphodon was primarily an insectivore or a piscivore, and Mark Witton argues that Dimorphodon was a specialized carnivore too large for an insectivorous diet, likely hunting small vertebrates despite its relatively weak jaw musculature.
Richard Owen speculated that Dimorphodon was a quadruped with a membrane between the tail and legs, making it ungainly on the ground.
